opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core problem is that large-scale historical events are, almost by definition, rare. If you want to train a system to forecast things like wars between great powers, revolutions, financial crises, or major technological transitions, you just don't have that many independent examples. There have been a handful of world wars, a modest number of great-power transitions, maybe dozens of really major financial crises depending on how you count. That's tiny compared to the millions or billions of examples we use to train models on other tasks.

And then the deeper problem is contamination. Any model trained on the internet already knows how history turned out. If you ask it, "In 1913, what's the probability of a general European war within two years?", it has read thousands of books about World War I. So you can't cleanly test whether it's forecasting or just remembering. That makes evaluation really hard, and it also makes training hard, because if you reward it for getting the "right" answer, you may just be rewarding retrieval of hindsight.

One approach people talk about is training models with strict knowledge cutoffs: build a model only on text available up to some date, say 1900 or 1950, and then see how well it predicts what came after. That's appealing, but there's a lot less digitized text from earlier periods, and it's skewed toward certain countries, languages, and elite perspectives. Keeping later information out is also surprisingly hard. Later editions, annotations, retrospective histories, and metadata leak in all over the place. Even the choice of which documents survived and got digitized is shaped by what later turned out to matter.

There's also a non-stationarity issue. The world of 1850 is quite different from the world of 2030 in terms of the speed of communication, the economy, nuclear weapons, and now AI itself. So even if you learn good patterns from historical data, it's unclear how much transfers to the situations we most care about, which may be genuinely unprecedented. An intelligence explosion or rapid AI-driven economic growth doesn't have a clean historical analog.

So I think the more promising path is a mix. Use the abundant data on smaller-scale, shorter-horizon forecasting questions, things like elections, economic indicators, and geopolitical questions on forecasting platforms, where you get fast feedback and can do proper out-of-sample testing on events after the training cutoff. That trains general forecasting skill and calibration. Then use the historical record more carefully, with cutoff-controlled models, as a supplement for the big-picture stuff. And as AI systems get better at reasoning, they can do a lot of the work a good human superforecaster does: base rates, reference classes, decomposing the question. That depends less on having a huge number of identical past examples and more on reasoning well with the examples you do have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the scarcity of historical events and smaller-scale forecasting questions, but does not identify individual workers’ outcomes as relatively independent training examples.

r002.rationale: It describes hindsight contamination and information leaks in historical documents, but not leakage from one macroeconomic outcome into correlated outcomes held back for testing.

r003.rationale: It proposes cutoff-controlled models trained only on older text, then evaluating how well they predict later events, using that approach as a supplement for big-picture forecasting.

fable-5.1.text:
The core problem is just scarcity. If you want to train a system to predict things like wars, financial crises, major technological transitions, regime changes — events that reshape the world — there haven't been that many of them. You might have a few dozen cases of the kind you care about over the span of recorded history, and the further back you go, the worse the records get and the less the underlying situation resembles anything you'd want to forecast today. So you don't have the millions of labelled examples that made image recognition or language modelling work. You have a tiny, noisy, non-stationary dataset.

And it's worse than just being small, because the events aren't independent draws from a stable distribution. The world in 1850 and the world in 1950 and the world today have different technologies, different institutions, different information environments. A model that fits the pattern of past industrial revolutions or past great-power wars may be learning things that have already stopped being true. Some of the most important things we'd like to forecast — the trajectory of AI itself, for instance — have essentially no historical precedent at all, so you're extrapolating from analogies rather than from instances of the thing.

Then there's the problem of what the data actually is. Historical records aren't neutral. They're written by particular people, with particular biases, about the things that happened to get recorded, and whole categories of relevant information — what decision-makers privately believed, what the counterfactuals were, the near misses that didn't become events — are just missing. For forecasting you really want to know the base rates of things that almost happened, and the historical record systematically under-represents those.

There's also a contamination issue that's specific to training large models. If a model has read all of history, it already knows how everything turned out. You can't straightforwardly test whether it would have predicted the fall of the Soviet Union from 1985 information, because it's seen 1991. You can try to do held-out evaluation — train with a cutoff date and then score on what came after — but then your test set is a few years of events, which is again very few data points, and you have to wait for new events to accumulate. Forecasting tournaments like Metaculus or the Good Judgment Project help here, because they generate a stream of resolved questions, but those questions skew towards things that resolve in months, not the decades-long structural shifts that matter most.

So I think the realistic path isn't that you train a model on a big dataset of historical events and it becomes a great forecaster from that supervision alone. It's more that you get systems that have very broad knowledge, good reasoning, the ability to build and check causal models, and that have been calibrated on the shorter-horizon questions where you do have feedback — and then you hope that the calibration and reasoning skill transfer to the rare, high-stakes cases. We should expect that transfer to be imperfect and to be the thing we scrutinise most carefully, because that's precisely where you can't check the answer until it's too late.

r001.rationale: The response describes a scarcity of historical events, but does not identify outcomes for individual workers as relatively independent training examples.

r002.rationale: It discusses contamination from a model having read history, but does not explain leakage from one macroeconomic outcome to correlated outcomes reserved for testing.

r003.rationale: It proposes held-out evaluation by training with a historical cutoff and scoring on later events, which validates forecasting using older data.

astra-6.text:
Well, one challenge is that there just aren’t that many independent examples. You can have a huge amount of text about a world war or an industrial revolution, but that doesn’t give you a huge number of world wars or industrial revolutions to learn from. And the events are connected, so you can’t simply treat every country in every year as an independent data point.

Another problem is hindsight. If you ask a model to forecast a historical event, it may already know what happened from its training data. Even if you remove explicit descriptions of the outcome, later writing can reveal it indirectly: which people are treated as important, which trends historians focus on, and so forth. It’s difficult to reconstruct the information available at the time without letting knowledge of the future creep in.

You could train models with information up to a particular date and then evaluate their forecasts of subsequent events. But that’s expensive to repeat, and for the really large, rare events you’re still going to have a small sample. If you evaluate prospectively, you have to wait for the outcomes.

So I think you’d want to get a lot of practice on more frequent, shorter-term questions where you can actually measure performance, and then investigate how well those skills transfer. But doing well on thousands of those questions wouldn’t, by itself, establish that a system can reliably forecast a major historical transformation.

r001.rationale: It describes few independent examples of major historical events and correlated country-year observations, but does not identify individual workers’ outcomes as training examples.

r002.rationale: The response discusses hindsight leakage about an event’s own outcome, but not leakage from one macroeconomic outcome to correlated outcomes held out for testing.

r003.rationale: It suggests training with information available up to a date, but does not propose validating macro-scale forecasting using a model trained to reason from older data.

sol-6.1.text:
One big challenge is that the number of genuinely independent examples is much smaller than the amount of text you have. You can have millions of pages about a war or a financial crisis, but those aren’t millions of separate observations of how wars or financial crises unfold. They’re many descriptions of the same event. And for some of the things we care most about, such as the development of advanced AI, we don’t have a set of closely comparable historical cases.

There’s also a serious problem with hindsight. If you ask a model to forecast an event from the perspective of someone in 1910, its training data will contain the outcome, as well as historical accounts that select the facts that turned out to matter. Even if you remove explicit statements of what happened, it’s difficult to establish that you’ve removed all that information. So doing well on that exercise might show that the model knows history, rather than that it can forecast.

A cleaner approach is to make predictions about events that haven’t happened yet and then score them as the outcomes arrive. But that takes time, especially for rare events and long time horizons. You can get much more feedback on shorter-term questions, and that can tell you something useful about a system’s forecasting abilities. The harder question is how much that performance carries over to the very unusual, consequential events we ultimately want to understand.

r001.rationale: It says many pages can describe the same event, but does not identify outcomes for individual workers as relatively independent examples.

r002.rationale: It discusses hindsight information leaking into a historical forecast, but not one macroeconomic outcome leaking information about correlated outcomes held out for testing.

r003.rationale: It proposes scoring predictions about future events; it does not propose validating macro-scale forecasting with a model trained on older data.
